newsitem.title: UK: Licht sees lower world sugar production for 1996/9.
newsitem.headline: Licht sees lower world sugar production for 1996/9.

text.p: World sugar production should reach 123.28 million tonnes raw value in 1996/97, down from the 125.76 million turned out in 1995/96, German statistician F.O. Licht said on Thursday.

In its second forecast of the world sugar balance, Licht said although there had been several changes to individual figures, output and consumption totals were little changed from the previous forecast last October.
In the first estimate, Licht pegged sugar production at 123.95 million tonnes for 1996/97 (September/October).
But it raised its forecast for indicated consumption by 0.6 percent to 120.29 million tonnes, after the 1995/96 figure of 116.92 million.
"Production is still well in excess of indicated consumption which points to a rise in stocks of 2.1 million tonnes," Licht said.

The stock/consumption ratio, although lower than the previous forecast, was forecast at 40.92 percent, the highest figure since 1985/86 when -- allowing for inflation -- prices were at a similarly low level.
It noted that the change had occurred in India and said the lower surplus figure would have little impact on world market prices.
Ending sugar stocks were expected to rise to 49.23 million tonnes from 47.12 million in 1995/96.
"It should be noted that the expected increase in surplus stocks will be heavily concentrated on the whites sector. This could impinge on the raw/white differential," Licht said.
The distinction between raw and white sugar was becoming cloudy with so much lower quality white sugar coming onto the market.
Gross import demand for sugar was forecast to fall by about 1.8 million tonnes from last year's 38.0 million tonnes, the report said.

"The big change will be in Asia where import demand is expected to fall from 15.2 to 13.7 million tonnes," it said, adding that the Philippines would be mainly responsible for the fall although Indonesia and China would also reduce their imports.
In Western Europe, Yugoslavia and Turkey would import less sugar than last year but higher U.S. imports would lead to an increase of more than 10 percent in north and central America, it added.
